# From one variable to two

_Source: ALPECOLE, University of Zurich_

## Today

- From the mean to the conditional mean
- Intercepts, slopes and residuals
- Fitting a line: least squares and `lm()`
- Reading and checking a model
- A warning: when one line misleads

## Last week: one variable

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.9}
ggplot(pengs, aes(x = seq_along(flipper_length_mm), y = flipper_length_mm)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(pengs$flipper_length_mm), colour = hornbill, linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(colour = pandan, alpha = 0.5, size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Penguin", y = "Flipper length (mm)")
```

The mean (`r round(mean(pengs$flipper_length_mm))` mm) is the simplest model of a variable: it predicts the same flipper length for every penguin. Most penguins are some distance away from it.

## Today: two variables

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.4}
ggplot(pengs, aes(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm)) +
  geom_point(colour = pandan, alpha = 0.35, size = 2) +
  stat_summary_bin(fun = mean, bins = 10, geom = "point",
                   colour = hornbill, size = 5) +
  stat_summary_bin(fun = mean, bins = 10, geom = "line",
                   colour = hornbill, linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Body mass (g)", y = "Flipper length (mm)")
```

If we know a penguin's body mass, we can do better: the [conditional mean]{.hl} is the mean flipper length of penguins with a given body mass (orange). The conditional means lie close to a straight line.

## Outcome and predictor

[Simple linear regression]{.hl} models one continuous outcome with one predictor (Winter, 2019).


:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="52%"}
- The __outcome__ (dependent or response variable, `y`) is what you measure
- The __predictor__ (independent variable, `x`) is what you manipulate, or measure alongside, to see whether the outcome changes with it
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
| Outcome | Predictor |
|:--|:--|
| Reaction time | Word frequency |
| Vowel duration | Speaking rate |
| Pitch (f0) | Speaker age |
| Reading speed | Font size |
:::

::::

# Intercepts & slopes

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` Alpine ibex climb near-vertical [slopes]{.hl}. In the Italian Alps, females scale the concrete walls of dams such as the Cingino dam to lick the salts that form on them.

_Source: Water Power Magazine_
:::

## The equation of a line

<div class="formula">y = b₀ + b₁ · x + e</div>

- `b₀`, the __intercept__: the value of `y` when `x = 0`
- `b₁`, the __slope__: how much `y` changes when `x` increases by 1
- `e`, the __error__ or __residual__: what the line does not explain

. . .

`b₀` and `b₁` are the model's [coefficients]{.hl}. Fitting a model means finding them.

## Same intercept, different slopes

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.6}
ggplot() +
  geom_abline(intercept = 3, slope = 1, colour = orchid, linewidth = 1.4) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 3, slope = -0.2, colour = kingfisher, linewidth = 1.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = moss) +
  annotate("point", x = 0, y = 3, colour = mist, size = 4) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.15, y = 2.6, label = "intercept = 3", colour = mist,
           hjust = 0, size = 5.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 2.6, y = 5.9, label = "slope = 1", colour = orchid, size = 5.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 5, y = 1.6, label = "slope = -0.2", colour = kingfisher, size = 5.5) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-1, 6), ylim = c(0, 6)) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "y")
```

## Different intercepts, same slope

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.6}
ggplot() +
  geom_abline(intercept = 5, slope = 0, colour = orchid, linewidth = 1.4) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 3, slope = 0, colour = kingfisher, linewidth = 1.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = moss) +
  annotate("point", x = 0, y = c(3, 5), colour = mist, size = 4) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.15, y = c(3.35, 5.35), label = c("intercept = 3", "intercept = 5"),
           colour = c(kingfisher, orchid), hjust = 0, size = 5.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 4.5, y = 4, label = "both slopes = 0", colour = mist, size = 5.5) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-1, 6), ylim = c(0, 6)) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "y")
```

## Fitting a line to data

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.6}
ggplot(pengs, aes(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm)) +
  geom_point(colour = pandan, alpha = 0.6, size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Body mass (g)", y = "Flipper length (mm)")
```

Heavier penguins have longer flippers. Which line describes this best?

## The regression line

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.6}
ggplot(pengs, aes(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm)) +
  geom_point(colour = pandan, alpha = 0.6, size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = hornbill, fill = hornbill, linewidth = 1.5) +
  labs(x = "Body mass (g)", y = "Flipper length (mm)")
```

`geom_smooth(method = "lm")` draws it. The band shows the uncertainty about the line.

## Residuals

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.4}
set.seed(4)
few <- augment(m) |> slice_sample(n = 30)
ggplot(few, aes(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = b0, slope = b1, colour = hornbill, linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = body_mass_g, yend = .fitted), colour = orchid, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(colour = pandan, size = 3) +
  labs(x = "Body mass (g)", y = "Flipper length (mm)")
```

<div class="formula">residual = observed − fitted</div>

## Least squares

One common method to estimate our __regression line__ is: __The least squares method__

. . .

It finds the line that minimises the sum of the squared residuals.

. . .

```{r}
sum(residuals(m)^2)                                  # the lm() line

guess <- 140 + 0.014 * pengs$body_mass_g             # another line
sum((pengs$flipper_length_mm - guess)^2)
```

. . .

Squaring makes all residuals positive, and penalises large misses more than small ones.

# Linear models in R

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` a male Alpine ibex weighs about 90 kg, and his horns grow to about 92 cm on average. A female weighs 35 to 49 kg, with horns of about 34 cm: one species, two very different [intercepts]{.hl}.

_Source: Gran Paradiso National Park_
:::

## `lm()` in `R`

`outcome ~ predictor`: "flipper length as a function of body mass"

```{r}
m <- lm(flipper_length_mm ~ body_mass_g, data = pengs)
m
```

. . .

`pengs` is `penguins` without missing values in these two columns, made with `drop_na()` from last week.

## `summary()` {.smaller}

```{r}
summary(m)
```

## Reading the coefficients

```{r}
coefficients(m)
```

. . .

- __Slope__: each extra gram adds `r round(b1, 4)` mm of flipper. Each extra kilogram adds `r round(b1 * 1000, 1)` mm.
- __Intercept__: a penguin weighing 0 g would have flippers of `r round(b0, 1)` mm.

. . .

The intercept is correct maths, but meaningless: there are no weightless penguins. Next week we fix this with [centering]{.hl}.

## Residuals average zero

```{r}
mean(residuals(m))
```

. . .

`e-16` means "times 10 to the power of −16": zero, up to rounding.

. . .

The line passes through the middle of the data: the points above it balance the points below it.

## `{broom}`: models as tibbles {.smaller}

```{r}
tidy(m)               # one row per coefficient
glance(m)[, 1:4]      # one row per model
augment(m)[, 1:4]     # one row per observation
```

. . .

Tibbles work with everything from `{dplyr}` and `{ggplot2}`.

## `R²`: how much does the model explain?

```{r}
glance(m)$r.squared
```

. . .

`R²` is the proportion of the variance in `y` that the model accounts for: `r round(r2 * 100)`% of the variation in flipper length goes with body mass.

. . .

- 0: the predictor tells us nothing about the outcome
- 1: every point lies exactly on the line
- In linguistics, much smaller values are normal: people are noisy

## Discussion

Body mass accounts for `r round(r2 * 100)`% of the variation in flipper length. Suppose a study finds that word frequency accounts for 5% of the variation in reaction times.

- Is that model useless?
- What might account for the other 95%?

## Predictions

```{r}
new_penguins <- tibble(body_mass_g = c(3000, 4000, 5000))
predict(m, newdata = new_penguins)
```

. . .

`fitted = b₀ + b₁ · x`: for 4000 g, `r round(b0, 1)` + `r round(b1, 4)` × 4000 = `r round(b0 + b1 * 4000, 1)` mm.

. . .

Only predict within the range of your data: `r min(pengs$body_mass_g)` to `r max(pengs$body_mass_g)` g. Outside it, the line is a guess.

# Checking the model

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` by the 19th century, Alpine ibex had been hunted out of the Alps except in the Italian king's hunting reserve, today [Gran Paradiso National Park]{.hl}. In the early 1900s, young ibex were smuggled from there into Switzerland, where the first reintroduction followed in 1911.

_Sources: Gran Paradiso National Park; Springer Nature Research Communities_
:::

## Checking the model: residuals

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.2}
ggplot(augment(m), aes(x = .resid)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = orchid, colour = floor_col) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = mist, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Residual (mm)", y = "Count")
```

Linear models assume residuals that are roughly normal: symmetric, centred on zero.

## Checking the model: constant variance

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.2}
ggplot(augment(m), aes(x = .fitted, y = .resid)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = mist, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(colour = kingfisher, alpha = 0.6, size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Fitted flipper length (mm)", y = "Residual (mm)")
```

They also assume residuals with roughly the same spread along the line: no funnel shapes. Chapter 4 covers both checks.

# Grouped data

The aim of the course is to teach __applied statistics__ for linguists (and social scientists)

```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width = "60%"}
if (file.exists("pb.png")) knitr::include_graphics("pb.png")
```

## A warning: three species again

Bill length by bill depth, all penguins together:

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.2}
bills <- drop_na(penguins, bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm)
ggplot(bills, aes(x = bill_depth_mm, y = bill_length_mm)) +
  geom_point(colour = pandan, alpha = 0.5, size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = mist, fill = mist, linewidth = 1.4) +
  labs(x = "Bill depth (mm)", y = "Bill length (mm)")
```

Deeper bills, shorter bills? The slope is negative.

## A warning: three species again

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.2}
ggplot(bills, aes(x = bill_depth_mm, y = bill_length_mm)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = species), alpha = 0.5, size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = mist, se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_smooth(aes(colour = species, fill = species), method = "lm", linewidth = 1.4) +
  labs(x = "Bill depth (mm)", y = "Bill length (mm)", colour = NULL, fill = NULL)
```

Within every species, the slope is positive. Ignoring species reversed the effect: this is [Simpson's paradox]{.hl}. Models with more than one predictor: watch this space.
